title: Endocrine Pathogens
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the microorganisms that injure endocrine glands and how they do it. Neisseria meningitidis causes bilateral adrenal hemorrhage through endotoxin-driven sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome). Pharyngeal bacteria cause acute suppurative thyroiditis, in children usually through a pyriform sinus fistula, while a preceding viral infection sets off subacute granulomatous thyroiditis. Tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, and cytomegalovirus destroy the adrenal glands and can cause Addison disease. Board questions describe an organism, a tissue lesion, or a hormonal picture and ask you to connect them, so the emphasis is on how each organism reaches the gland and how the damage explains the signs and laboratory findings.

connections.how: The adrenal arterial plexus that drains through a single central vein explains why sepsis and coagulopathy cause adrenal hemorrhage.
A persistent tract from the caudal pharyngeal pouches gives pharyngeal bacteria a direct route to the left thyroid lobe.
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis must be separated from painless, postpartum, and Hashimoto thyroiditis by pain, ESR, and radioiodine uptake.
Infectious adrenalitis is one cause of primary adrenal insufficiency, alongside the more common autoimmune form.

connections.to: Systemic pathogens and acquired immunodeficiency (IM-14, IM-15-B)
connections.how: Complement deficiency and advanced HIV infection explain who is susceptible to meningococcemia and to cytomegalovirus adrenalitis.

blocks.text: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus whose paired cells have flattened, kidney-bean shaped facing sides. It is oxidase positive, grows on chocolate agar, and ferments both glucose and maltose, which separates it from Neisseria gonorrhoeae (glucose only). It spreads by respiratory droplets and close contact, colonizes the nasopharynx of a minority of healthy people, and causes outbreaks where young adults live closely together, such as dormitories and military barracks.

blocks.title: Meningococcal virulence factors
rows: Attach to nonciliated nasopharyngeal epithelial cells
Cleaves secretory IgA1 at the mucosal surface
Blocks phagocytosis and complement deposition in blood; defines serogroups (A, B, C, W, X, Y)
Lipid A endotoxin; shed in large amounts in outer membrane blebs
blocks.caption: Each factor matches one step of invasion or injury.

blocks.text: Once the organism crosses the mucosa, survival in blood depends on the capsule, and clearance depends on antibody plus complement assembling the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9) on the outer membrane. Deficiency of terminal complement components or properdin therefore predisposes to recurrent neisserial bacteremia, and asplenia removes a major site of clearance of encapsulated bacteria.
From endotoxin to adrenal hemorrhage

Continuous shedding of blebs makes blood endotoxin levels in meningococcemia among the highest of any infection. Lipid A binds TLR4 with its coreceptors MD-2 and CD14 on monocytes and macrophages and activates NF-kB, driving release of TNF-alpha, IL-1, and IL-6. These cytokines cause vasodilation and capillary leak, and they induce tissue factor on monocytes and endothelium while suppressing thrombomodulin and the protein C pathway. Coagulation is switched on throughout the microcirculation: microthrombi form, platelets and clotting factors are consumed, and bleeding follows. This is disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Thrombosis in dermal vessels produces the petechial rash that can progress to purpura fulminans.

The adrenal gland is especially vulnerable because of its vascular design. Superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries form a rich subcapsular plexus that feeds cortical sinusoids, and all of this blood leaves through a single central vein. Thrombosis of the venous outflow in DIC, together with damaged capillaries, causes hemorrhagic infarction of both glands. The sudden loss of cortisol removes its permissive support of vascular tone and catecholamine responsiveness, so hypotension stops responding to fluids. Because the loss is abrupt, ACTH has no time to cause hyperpigmentation.

blocks.title: Meningococcemia to Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
steps: Droplet spread; pili attach in the nasopharynx
Organism invades blood; capsule resists phagocytosis
Bacteria shed LOS-rich outer membrane blebs
Lipid A binds TLR4; TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 released
Tissue factor up, protein C pathway down: DIC
Adrenal venous thrombosis and hemorrhagic infarction, both glands
Acute cortisol loss deepens septic shock
blocks.caption: The causal chain from colonization to adrenal failure.

blocks.text: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is classically meningococcal but also occurs in sepsis from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Staphylococcus aureus. Acute adrenal insufficiency worsens the shock, although how much it drives the shock rather than marks its severity is debated.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the laboratory picture
blocks.text: A 19-year-old in a dormitory develops fever of 39.5 °C (103.1 °F), spreading purpura, and hypotension despite fluids. Platelets are low, PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low, and D-dimer is high: consumption of platelets and factors with active fibrinolysis means DIC. Low sodium with high potassium suggests adrenal loss, although sepsis-related acidosis and kidney injury can also raise potassium. Blood culture grows gram-negative diplococci. Both problems trace back to lipid A: tissue factor drives DIC, and DIC infarcts glands that drain through a single vein.

blocks.predict: Predict the infection risk in a patient who lacks C7.
blocks.explain: Blood-borne Neisseria are killed mainly by the membrane attack complex, so lacking C7 causes recurrent neisserial bacteremia, while C3b opsonization still protects against most other bacteria.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on clearance in blood.

sections.title: Acute suppurative thyroiditis and the pyriform sinus fistula

blocks.text: Bacterial infection of the thyroid is rare because the gland resists it well. It is enclosed in a fibrous capsule, has a very rich blood supply and lymphatic drainage, and its follicles contain high concentrations of iodide along with the hydrogen peroxide used for hormone synthesis. Infection therefore usually needs a special route or a weakened gland: a pyriform sinus fistula in children, or preexisting nodular goiter, thyroid cancer, needle aspiration, or immunosuppression in adults.

The usual organisms are those of the skin and upper airway. They are told apart by Gram stain and simple tests, summarized below. When a fistula connects the gland to the pharynx, mixed oropharyngeal flora including anaerobes is also common.

blocks.title: Bacteria of acute suppurative thyroiditis
rows: Catalase negative, optochin sensitive, bile soluble
blocks.caption: The three classic causes. All produce neutrophilic inflammation and abscess.

blocks.text: The pyriform sinus fistula

The pyriform sinus is the recess of the laryngopharynx on each side of the laryngeal inlet. A pyriform sinus fistula is a remnant of the caudal pharyngeal pouches (the third or, more often, the fourth) that persists as a tract from the apex of the sinus down to the region of the upper thyroid lobe. It occurs on the left in the large majority of cases. Pharyngeal bacteria travel down the tract, often after an upper respiratory infection inflames the pharynx, and seed the left lobe.

blocks.title: Recurrent left-sided thyroid abscess in a child
steps: Caudal pharyngeal pouch remnant persists as a tract
Tract runs from left pyriform sinus to thyroid
Upper respiratory infection inflames the pharynx
Oropharyngeal bacteria track down the tract
Neutrophilic abscess forms in the left lobe
Infection recurs while the tract remains
blocks.caption: Why the same side becomes infected again and again.

blocks.text: The mechanism explains the presentation: fever, a tender, warm, sometimes fluctuant anterior neck swelling and pain on swallowing. Because bacteria destroy a limited region rather than the whole gland, thyroid function is usually normal, although destruction of follicles occasionally releases enough stored hormone to cause transient thyrotoxicosis. The abscess takes up little radioiodine, so it appears as a cold area on a scan. A second left-sided thyroid infection in a child is the classic clue to a fistula, which is usually demonstrated by contrast swallow once the inflammation settles.

blocks.predict: Why would a right-sided thyroid abscess in a child without prior neck surgery make a fistula less likely?
blocks.explain: Pyriform sinus fistulas arise almost always on the left, so a right-sided abscess suggests another route such as bloodstream seeding, local trauma, or an abnormal gland.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on the pyriform sinus fistula.

sections.title: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis after viral infection

blocks.text: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain thyroiditis) is a painful, self-limited inflammation of the thyroid that typically begins about 2 to 8 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. It is most common in women aged about 30 to 50 years. Coxsackievirus and mumps virus are the classic associations; adenovirus, influenza virus, echovirus, measles virus, and others have also been implicated. Virus is rarely recovered from the gland itself, which suggests that the injury is driven by the host response rather than by ongoing viral replication.

blocks.title: Viruses classically linked to subacute thyroiditis
rows: Group A: herpangina, hand-foot-and-mouth disease; group B: myocarditis, pericarditis, pleurodynia
blocks.caption: Coxsackievirus spreads by fecal-oral and respiratory routes; mumps spreads by respiratory droplets.

blocks.text: The leading model is that viral antigen, or thyroid antigen released from virus-damaged cells, stimulates cytotoxic T cells in genetically susceptible people. The strongest genetic link is HLA-B35, an MHC class I allele, which fits a CD8 T cell response against follicular cells. The T cells destroy follicular epithelium, and colloid leaks into the interstitium.

Histology follows the time course. Early lesions show disrupted follicles and neutrophils, sometimes forming microabscesses. Later, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages gather, and multinucleated giant cells surround and engulf fragments of extravasated colloid, forming granulomas. These granulomas are noncaseating and centered on follicles, and the gland eventually heals with patchy fibrosis.

blocks.title: Thyroid function in subacute thyroiditis
steps: Follicles destroyed; stored T4 and T3 leak into blood
Thyrotoxic phase: TSH suppressed, radioiodine uptake very low
Stores exhausted: brief euthyroid phase
Hypothyroid phase while follicles regenerate
Recovery to normal function in most patients
blocks.caption: Hormone release is passive leakage, not new synthesis, which explains low uptake during thyrotoxicosis.

blocks.text: The manifestations follow from this mechanism. Inflammation stretches the thyroid capsule, producing neck pain that radiates to the jaw or ear and a firm, very tender gland, with fever, malaise, and a markedly raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein. Leakage of preformed hormone causes thyrotoxicosis with a relatively high T4 to T3 ratio, reflecting the composition of stored hormone, and a high serum thyroglobulin. Because TSH is suppressed and damaged follicles cannot trap iodide, 24-hour radioiodine uptake is very low, the key contrast with Graves disease, in which TSH receptor antibodies drive high uptake. A minority of patients remain permanently hypothyroid.

Two distinctions are tested often. Painless (silent) and postpartum thyroiditis also cause low-uptake thyrotoxicosis, but they are autoimmune lymphocytic processes with no pain, a normal ESR, and often anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies. Acute suppurative thyroiditis is painful too, but it is a localized bacterial abscess with usually normal thyroid function.

blocks.title: Worked example: two painful thyroids
blocks.text: Patient A has fever and a fluctuant, tender left thyroid swelling; TSH and free T4 are normal and the swelling is cold on scan. Patient B had a cold 4 weeks ago and now has a diffusely tender gland, low TSH, high free T4, ESR of 80 mm/h, and 24-hour radioiodine uptake under 5 percent. In A, a localized bacterial abscess spares most follicles, so function is normal. In B, T cell destruction across the gland releases stored hormone, suppressing TSH, and the injured follicles cannot trap iodide, so uptake is low. A is acute suppurative thyroiditis; B is subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

The adrenal cortex has a large functional reserve, so cortisol and aldosterone fall only after about 90 percent of the cortex in both glands is destroyed. A disease must therefore reach both glands, and infections do this by hematogenous spread. Autoimmune adrenalitis is the most common cause of Addison disease in developed countries, but tuberculosis is the leading cause worldwide and was the cause in Addison's original cases.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing, obligately aerobic rod whose cell wall is rich in mycolic acids, so it resists decolorization with acid alcohol and stains as acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen stain). It seeds the adrenals during hematogenous spread from the lung. Inside macrophages it blocks phagosome-lysosome fusion. Th1 cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages and organizes granulomas maintained by TNF-alpha; the centers undergo caseous necrosis. Caseating granulomas replace cortex and medulla alike, so early disease enlarges the glands, and healed disease leaves small, often calcified glands.

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus that grows as a mold in soil contaminated by bird and bat droppings, especially in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, and as a small yeast (about 2 to 4 µm) at body temperature. Inhaled spores convert to yeasts that multiply inside macrophages, which carry them through the blood. In disseminated histoplasmosis the adrenals are a frequent target, and granulomatous destruction often enlarges both glands. Other endemic fungi, notably Paracoccidioides brasiliensis in South America, can act the same way.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is an enveloped, double-stranded DNA herpesvirus that establishes latency and reactivates when cellular immunity fails, usually at CD4 counts below 50 cells per microliter in AIDS. It is the most common adrenal infection found at autopsy in AIDS. Infected cells enlarge and carry owl's eye intranuclear inclusions, and the necrotizing adrenalitis often begins in the medulla and spreads into the adjacent cortex. Because it seldom destroys 90 percent of the cortex, overt Addison disease from CMV alone is uncommon.

blocks.title: Infectious causes of adrenalitis
rows: Caseating granulomas; enlarged then calcified glands
Endemic areas; reactivation or miliary disease
Dimorphic fungus; small yeasts in macrophages
Enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus; owl's eye inclusions
Necrotizing adrenalitis, medulla and inner cortex
AIDS with CD4 below about 50 per microliter
blocks.caption: All three spread through the blood and involve both glands and the medulla, unlike autoimmune adrenalitis, which leaves small glands and spares the medulla.

blocks.title: Tuberculous Addison disease
steps: Blood-borne M. tuberculosis seeds both adrenals
Th1 and macrophages form caseating granulomas
Granulomas replace cortex and medulla
About 90 percent cortex lost: cortisol and aldosterone fall
Low cortisol raises CRH and POMC-derived ACTH
Excess ACTH stimulates melanocortin 1 receptors: hyperpigmentation
blocks.caption: Granulomatous destruction produces the full hormonal picture of primary adrenal insufficiency.

blocks.text: The manifestations follow from the lost hormones. Cortisol deficiency causes fatigue, weight loss, hypotension, and fasting hypoglycemia. Aldosterone deficiency causes sodium wasting, volume depletion, salt craving, hyperkalemia, and a mild non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, with high renin. Chronic ACTH excess darkens skin creases, scars, and buccal mucosa. Laboratory confirmation rests on low morning cortisol with high ACTH and a poor cortisol response to synthetic ACTH.

blocks.predict: Would a patient with adrenal insufficiency from pituitary failure show hyperpigmentation or hyperkalemia?
blocks.explain: No. ACTH is low, so there is no melanocortin drive to pigment, and aldosterone is preserved because the renin-angiotensin system, not ACTH, is its main regulator, so potassium stays normal.
blocks.check: Compare with the tuberculous Addison disease flow and the final paragraph of this section.

integration.text: Each infection in this chapter is explained by joining anatomy, microbiology, immunology, and pathology. Adrenal vascular anatomy, with a rich arterial plexus draining through one vein, turns lipid A-driven DIC into bilateral hemorrhagic infarction. Pharyngeal pouch embryology turns ordinary throat flora into a recurrent left-sided thyroid abscess. HLA class I genetics and cytotoxic T cells turn a common viral illness into granulomatous destruction of follicles, and Th1 granuloma formation, or loss of T cell immunity in AIDS, determines which organisms destroy the adrenal cortex.

The endocrine consequence then depends on how much of the gland is lost and how fast. Sudden bilateral adrenal hemorrhage causes crisis without pigment change; slow granulomatous destruction causes Addison disease with hyperpigmentation; focal thyroid abscess spares function, while diffuse follicle damage releases stored hormone. Limits matter: most Addison disease in developed countries is autoimmune, CMV adrenalitis is frequent but rarely sufficient alone, and a viral cause of subacute thyroiditis is usually inferred from history rather than proven in the gland.

summary: Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative, oxidase-positive diplococcus that ferments glucose and maltose and spreads by respiratory droplets.
Pili attach, IgA1 protease protects at the mucosa, the capsule protects in blood, and LOS lipid A causes the injury.
Terminal complement (C5 to C9) or properdin deficiency and asplenia predispose to meningococcal bacteremia.
Lipid A binds TLR4, cytokines induce tissue factor and suppress protein C, and DIC follows.
Adrenal arteries feed a plexus drained by one central vein, so DIC causes bilateral hemorrhagic infarction and shock unresponsive to fluids.
Acute suppurative thyroiditis is usually Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, or Streptococcus pneumoniae, with normal thyroid function.
Recurrent left-sided thyroid abscess in a child points to a pyriform sinus fistula from the caudal pharyngeal pouches.
Subacute thyroiditis follows a viral infection such as coxsackievirus or mumps, is linked to HLA-B35, and shows a painful gland, high ESR, and very low radioiodine uptake.

Infectious Addison disease needs about 90 percent loss of both cortices: tuberculosis (caseating granulomas, calcification), histoplasmosis (bilateral enlargement), and CMV in AIDS (owl's eye inclusions, rarely sufficient alone).
